claim: In rat optic nerve, the node of Ranvier length varies over a 4.4-fold range.
source: We now show that, in rat optic nerve and cerebral cortical axons, the node of Ranvier length varies over a 4.4-fold and 8.7-fold range respectively
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: In rat cerebral cortical axons, the node of Ranvier length varies over an 8.7-fold range.
source: We now show that, in rat optic nerve and cerebral cortical axons, the node of Ranvier length varies over a 4.4-fold and 8.7-fold range respectively
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: Variation of node length is much less along axons than between axons.
source: We now show that, in rat optic nerve and cerebral cortical axons, the node of Ranvier length varies over a 4.4-fold and 8.7-fold range respectively and that variation of the node length is much less along axons than between axons.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by data in Figure 2 showing measurements along individual axons.

claim: Node length differences will alter conduction speed by approximately 20%.
source: Modelling predicts that these node length differences will alter conduction speed by ~20%, similar to the changes produced by altering the number of myelin wraps or the internode length.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results presented in Figure 3.

claim: Node length changes produce conduction speed changes similar to those produced by altering the number of myelin wraps.
source: Modelling predicts that these node length differences will alter conduction speed by ~20%, similar to the changes produced by altering the number of myelin wraps or the internode length.
evidence: This comparison is based on computational modeling results.

claim: Node length changes produce conduction speed changes similar to those produced by altering internode length.
source: Modelling predicts that these node length differences will alter conduction speed by ~20%, similar to the changes produced by altering the number of myelin wraps or the internode length.
evidence: This comparison is based on computational modeling results.

claim: For a given change of conduction speed, the membrane area change needed at the node is more than 270-fold less than that needed in the myelin sheath.
source: For a given change of conduction speed, the membrane area change needed at the node is >270-fold less than that needed in the myelin sheath.
evidence: This is calculated from modeling results and presented in Figure 3G.

claim: Axon-specific adjustment of node of Ranvier length is potentially an energy-efficient mechanism for tuning the arrival time of information in the CNS.
source: Thus, axon-specific adjustment of node of Ranvier length is potentially an energy-efficient and rapid mechanism for tuning the arrival time of information in the CNS.
evidence: This is inferred from the modeling results showing smaller membrane area changes are needed compared to myelin alterations.

claim: Axon-specific adjustment of node of Ranvier length is potentially a rapid mechanism for tuning the arrival time of information in the CNS.
source: Thus, axon-specific adjustment of node of Ranvier length is potentially an energy-efficient and rapid mechanism for tuning the arrival time of information in the CNS.
evidence: This is speculated based on the smaller membrane area changes needed compared to myelin alterations.

claim: An adjustment of myelin thickness may be used to tune the conduction speed of myelinated axons during development or learning.
source: During development or learning, an adjustment of myelin thickness or internode length may be used to tune the conduction speed of myelinated axons (Fields, 2008; Tomassy et al., 2014; Ullén, 2009; Kimura and Itami, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: An adjustment of internode length may be used to tune the conduction speed of myelinated axons during development or learning.
source: During development or learning, an adjustment of myelin thickness or internode length may be used to tune the conduction speed of myelinated axons (Fields, 2008; Tomassy et al., 2014; Ullén, 2009; Kimura and Itami, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Tuning conduction speed can promote synchronous neuronal firing.
source: This can promote synchronous neuronal firing (Lang and Rosenbluth, 2003; Sugihara et al., 1993)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Tuning conduction speed can make impulse propagation time less dependent on the spatial trajectory of the axon transmitting information between areas.
source: make impulse propagation time less dependent on the spatial trajectory of the axon transmitting information between areas (Salami et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Tuning conduction speed can adjust propagation delays to mediate sound localization.
source: or adjust propagation delays to mediate sound localization (Carr and Konishi, 1990; McAlpine and Grothe, 2003; Seidl et al., 2010; Ford et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Magnetic resonance imaging of humans suggests that myelination can increase while learning motor tasks such as piano playing.
source: Magnetic resonance imaging of humans and cellular studies of rodents suggest that myelination can increase while learning motor tasks such as piano playing (Bengtsson et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Cellular studies of rodents suggest that myelination can increase while learning juggling.
source: Magnetic resonance imaging of humans and cellular studies of rodents suggest that myelination can increase while learning motor tasks such as piano playing (Bengtsson et al., 2005), juggling (Scholz et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Cellular studies of rodents suggest that myelination can increase while learning reaching.
source: reaching (Sampaio-Baptista et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Cellular studies of rodents suggest that myelination can increase while learning running.
source: running (McKenzie et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Increasing the length of the node will increase the node capacitance.
source: Increasing the length of the node will increase the node capacitance and the axial resistance for current flow into the internode, which will both decrease conduction speed.
evidence: This is based on established biophysical principles.

claim: Increasing the length of the node will increase the axial resistance for current flow into the internode.
source: Increasing the length of the node will increase the node capacitance and the axial resistance for current flow into the internode, which will both decrease conduction speed.
evidence: This is based on established biophysical principles.

claim: Increased node capacitance and axial resistance will both decrease conduction speed.
source: Increasing the length of the node will increase the node capacitance and the axial resistance for current flow into the internode, which will both decrease conduction speed.
evidence: This is based on established biophysical principles.

claim: A greater node length could increase the number of voltage-gated Na+ channels at the node if the channel density is constant.
source: On the other hand, a greater length could increase the number of voltage-gated Na+ channels at the node (if the channel density is constant), which may increase conduction speed.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the relationship between area and channel number at constant density.

claim: An increased number of voltage-gated Na+ channels at the node may increase conduction speed.
source: On the other hand, a greater length could increase the number of voltage-gated Na+ channels at the node (if the channel density is constant), which may increase conduction speed.
evidence: This is based on established understanding of action potential propagation.

claim: The mean node length in adult rat optic nerve measured by electron microscopy was 1.08 ± 0.02 µm (n = 46 nodes).
source: Using electron microscopy (EM) we found the mean node length was 1.08 ± 0.02 µm (mean ± s.e.m., n = 46 nodes).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from electron microscopy data.

claim: Node lengths in adult rat optic nerve varied 2-fold, from 0.7 to 1.4 µm with a standard deviation of 0.15 µm.
source: Node lengths varied 2-fold, from 0.7 to 1.4 µm with a standard deviation of 0.15 µm (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on electron microscopy measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Node lengths in adult rat optic nerve were not significantly correlated with axon diameter at the node.
source: Node lengths were not significantly correlated with axon diameter at the node, which had a mean value of 0.80 ± 0.03 µm (standard deviation 0.19 µm; Figure 1—figure supplement 1, the slope of the regression line is not significantly different from zero, p=0.46).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mean axon diameter at the node in adult rat optic nerve was 0.80 ± 0.03 µm (standard deviation 0.19 µm).
source: Node lengths were not significantly correlated with axon diameter at the node, which had a mean value of 0.80 ± 0.03 µm (standard deviation 0.19 µm; Figure 1—figure supplement 1, the slope of the regression line is not significantly different from zero, p=0.46).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from electron microscopy data.

claim: The different node lengths observed in adult rat optic nerve did not simply reflect axons being of different sizes.
source: Thus, the different node lengths observed did not simply reflect axons being of different sizes.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between node length and axon diameter.

claim: Using confocal microscopy, the mean node length in adult rat optic nerve was 1.02 ± 0.02 μm (standard deviation 0.29 µm, n = 164).
source: We again found node length variability (Figure 1C,E,F,H), the mean node length was not significantly different (p=0.06) from that obtained with EM (1.02 ± 0.02 μm, standard deviation 0.29 µm, n = 164, Figure 1E)
evidence: This is a direct measurement from confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The mean node length measured by confocal microscopy in adult rat optic nerve was not significantly different from that obtained with EM (p=0.06).
source: the mean node length was not significantly different (p=0.06) from that obtained with EM (1.02 ± 0.02 μm, standard deviation 0.29 µm, n = 164, Figure 1E)
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of confocal and EM measurements.

claim: In adult rat optic nerve measured by confocal microscopy, there was no significant dependence of node length on node diameter (p=0.14).
source: and there was again no significant dependence on either node diameter (Figure 1H, p=0.14)
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: In adult rat optic nerve measured by confocal microscopy, there was no significant dependence of node length on axon diameter at the paranode (p=0.89).
source: or axon diameter at the paranode (measured as the diameter of the Caspr labelling: p=0.89)
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of confocal microscopy data.

claim: In the grey matter of adult rat cerebral cortex (layer V of motor cortex), node lengths ranged from 0.43 to 3.72 µm (mean value ± s.e.m 1.50 ± 0.05, standard deviation 0.58 µm, n = 158).
source: In the grey matter of the adult cerebral cortex (layer V of motor cortex) an even larger, 8.7-fold, range of node lengths was observed (Figure 1D,E,G,H), from 0.43 to 3.72 µm (mean value ± s.e.m 1.50 ± 0.05, standard deviation 0.58 µm, n = 158).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1.

claim: In adult rat cerebral cortex layer V, there was no significant dependence of node length on node diameter (p=0.42).
source: Again there was no significant dependence on node diameter (Figure 1H, p=0.42)
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The mean node diameter in adult rat cerebral cortex layer V was 0.64 ± 0.01 µm (n = 158, standard deviation 0.14 µm).
source: the mean value of which was 0.64 ± 0.01 µm (n = 158, standard deviation 0.14 µm)
evidence: This is a direct measurement from confocal microscopy data.

claim: In adult rat cerebral cortex layer V, there was no significant dependence of node length on axon diameter at the paranode (p=0.98).
source: or on axon diameter at the paranode (p=0.98)
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of confocal microscopy data.

claim: Variability of node length is a general feature of myelinated axons.
source: Thus, variability of node length is a general feature of myelinated axons.
evidence: This is inferred from observations in both optic nerve and cortex.

claim: The greater variability of node length observed in the cortex than in the optic nerve has parallels with the far greater variability of myelination seen in the adult cortex.
source: The greater variability of node length observed in the cortex than in the optic nerve has parallels with the far greater variability of myelination seen in the adult cortex (Tomassy et al., 2014)
evidence: This comparison is made with reference to previous literature on myelination variability.

claim: Greater variability of node length in cortex could reflect tuning of individual axon conduction speeds to meet information processing needs.
source: and could reflect tuning of individual axon conduction speeds to meet information processing needs.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed variability.

claim: There is a linear correlation between summed NaV1.6 staining and node length in cortex (p=1.2×10−15).
source: We found that there is a linear correlation between summed NaV1.6 staining and node length (p=1.2×10−15)
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The number of sodium channels at nodes is approximately proportional to node length.
source: indicating that the number of sodium channels at nodes is approximately proportional to node length (cf. Rios et al., 2003)
evidence: This is inferred from the linear correlation between NaV1.6 staining and node length, with reference to previous literature.

claim: Larger nodes are generated by the insertion of more NaV-containing membrane.
source: consistent with larger nodes being generated by the insertion of more NaV-containing membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the proportionality between sodium channel number and node length.

claim: At any given sodium channel labelling intensity there was still a large variation in node lengths.
source: However, at any given sodium channel labelling intensity there was still a large variation in node lengths
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Sodium channel density is not absolutely constant across nodes.
source: suggesting that sodium channel density is not absolutely constant
evidence: This is inferred from the variation in node lengths at given channel labeling intensities.

claim: It may be possible to vary node length in a manner independent of sodium channel number.
source: and that it may be possible to vary node length in a manner independent of sodium channel number.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed variation in node lengths at given channel labeling intensities.

claim: Along individual axons in the corpus callosum, the distribution of node lengths was much narrower than that observed over all callosal axons examined.
source: Remarkably, along individual axons (Figure 2B,C), the distribution of node lengths was much narrower than that observed over all callosal axons examined (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is based on measurements from dye-filled axons shown in Figure 2.

claim: Along individual axons in the corpus callosum, the coefficient of variation for node length was 48.8% ± 3.5% lower than that observed over all axons (p=1.1×10−10, n = 18 axons).
source: with a 48.8% ± 3.5% lower coefficient of variation (s.d./mean, Figure 2D, p=1.1×10−10, one sample t-test, n = 18 axons).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of measurements from dye-filled axons shown in Figure 2.

claim: Even when excluding axons with mean node lengths >2.25 µm, the coefficient of variation for single axons was 38.8% ± 4.7% lower than that observed over all axons (p=6.6×10−7).
source: Importantly, even when excluding axons with mean node lengths >2.25 µm (which were found less frequently, as predicted by the distribution in Figure 1G–H), the coefficient of variation for single axons was 38.8% ± 4.7% lower than that observed over all axons (p=6.6×10−7).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of a subset of the dye-filled axon data.

claim: Node length was not correlated with internode length (p=0.1).
source: Node length was not correlated with internode length (p=0.1, Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of measurements from dye-filled axons shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Node lengths are similar along axons but differ significantly between axons.
source: Thus, node lengths are similar along axons but differ significantly between axons.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing lower coefficient of variation within axons than between axons.

claim: Individual axons may consistently adjust their node length to tune conduction speed.
source: This raises the possibility that individual axons consistently adjust their node length to tune conduction speed.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that node lengths are similar along individual axons.

claim: The conduction speed predicted for the mean node length in optic nerve was 2.95 m/s.
source: The conduction speeds predicted for the mean node lengths observed (2.95 m/s for the optic nerve and 2.61 m/s for the cortex)
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling.

claim: The conduction speed predicted for the mean node length in cortical grey matter was 2.61 m/s.
source: The conduction speeds predicted for the mean node lengths observed (2.95 m/s for the optic nerve and 2.61 m/s for the cortex)
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling.

claim: The predicted conduction speeds were within the range of values observed experimentally in the adult rat optic nerve (2.5–15 m/s).
source: were within the range of values observed experimentally in the adult rat optic nerve (2.5–15 m/s: Foster et al. (1982); Sefton and Swinburn (1964); Sjöström et al. (1985))
evidence: This comparison is made with reference to previous experimental literature.

claim: The predicted conduction speeds were within the range of values observed for different classes of rat cortical grey matter output axons (1.8–5.9 m/s).
source: and for different classes of rat cortical grey matter output axons (1.8–5.9 m/s: Kelly et al., 2001).
evidence: This comparison is made with reference to previous experimental literature.

claim: When the number of channels was held constant at each node, the predicted conduction speed falls with increasing node length.
source: Figure 3A and B show that, when the number of channels was held constant at each node, the predicted conduction speed falls with increasing node length (dashed curves).
evidence: This is shown by modeling results in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The decrease in conduction speed with increasing node length (when channel number is constant) occurs because the increase in node length increases the nodal capacitance.
source: This occurs for two reasons: the increase in node length increases the nodal capacitance (so each node takes longer to charge), and the intracellular axial resistance to current flow from the node into the internode is increased.
evidence: This is an explanation based on biophysical principles applied to the modeling results.

claim: The decrease in conduction speed with increasing node length (when channel number is constant) occurs because the intracellular axial resistance to current flow from the node into the internode is increased.
source: This occurs for two reasons: the increase in node length increases the nodal capacitance (so each node takes longer to charge), and the intracellular axial resistance to current flow from the node into the internode is increased.
evidence: This is an explanation based on biophysical principles applied to the modeling results.

claim: For optic nerve axons with constant channel number, increasing the node length from 1.02 µm to 2.2 µm is predicted to decrease the conduction speed by 6.5%.
source: Increasing the node length from its mean value of 1.02 µm to the largest value observed (2.2 µm) is predicted to decrease the conduction speed by 6.5%
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figure 3A.

claim: For optic nerve axons with constant channel number, decreasing the node length from 1.02 µm to 0.5 µm increases the speed by 3.2%.
source: while decreasing the node length to the smallest value measured (0.5 µm) increases the speed by 3.2%
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figure 3A.

claim: For optic nerve axons with constant channel number, the speed at node length 0.5 µm is 10.3% larger than at a length of 2.2 µm.
source: (giving a speed that is 10.3% larger than at a length of 2.2 µm).
evidence: This is calculated from the modeling results.

claim: For cortical axons with constant channel number, the predicted changes in conduction speed with node length are larger than for optic nerve.
source: For cortical axons (Figure 3B) the predicted changes are larger
evidence: This is observed by comparing modeling results in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: The larger predicted changes in cortical axons are partly because, with a 1.5-fold longer node and a 1.7-fold shorter internode length, the nodal membrane contributes a larger fraction of the total membrane capacitance (14% in cortical axons versus 8% in optic nerve axons).
source: partly because, with a 1.5-fold longer node and a 1.7-fold shorter internode length, the nodal membrane contributes a larger fraction of the total membrane capacitance (14% in cortical axons versus 8% in optic nerve axons).
evidence: This is an explanation based on the geometrical parameters used in the model.

claim: For cortical axons with constant channel number, the node length variation from 0.43 µm to 3.7 µm results in conduction speeds that are 11.6% slower (for the longest node) and 7% faster (for the shortest node) than the speed for the mean node length of 1.5 µm.
source: The node length variation observed in rat cortex (Figure 1G–H and 0.43 µm to 3.7 µm) results in conduction speeds that are 11.6% slower (for the longest node) and 7% faster (for the shortest node) than the speed for the mean node length of 1.5 µm.
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figure 3B.

claim: For cortical axons with constant channel number, altering node length from 3.7 to 0.43 µm would increase the speed by approximately 21%.
source: Thus, altering node length from 3.7 to 0.43 µm would increase the speed by approximately 21%.
evidence: This is calculated from the modeling results.

claim: When the nodal ion channel density is kept constant, the plot of speed against node length shows a maximum.
source: Consequently, the plot of speed against node length shows a maximum (solid curves in Figure 3A–B: note that, above this maximum, increasing node length decreases speed for the reasons stated above, despite the increase in number of sodium channels at the node).
evidence: This is shown by modeling results in Figure 3A and B.

claim: For optic nerve axons with constant channel density, decreasing the node length from 1.02 µm to 0.5 µm is predicted to decrease conduction speed by 14.1%.
source: Decreasing the optic nerve node length from its mean value of 1.02 µm to the lowest length observed (0.5 µm) is predicted to decrease conduction speed by 14.1%
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figure 3A.

claim: For optic nerve axons with constant channel density, increasing node length from 1.02 µm to 1.7 µm increases the speed by 3.3%.
source: while increasing node length to the value generating the maximum conduction speed (1.7 µm) increases the speed by 3.3% (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figure 3A.

claim: For optic nerve axons with constant channel density, the speed at node length 1.7 µm is 20.2% higher than at a length of 0.5 µm.
source: to a value that is 20.2% higher than at a length of 0.5 µm.
evidence: This is calculated from the modeling results.

claim: For cortical axons with constant channel density, decreasing the node length from 1.5 µm to 0.43 µm decreases the conduction velocity by 19.6%.
source: Similarly, for the cortex, decreasing the node length from the mean value of 1.5 µm to the smallest observed value of 0.43 µm decreases the conduction velocity by 19.6%
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figure 3B.

claim: For cortical axons with constant channel density, increasing the node length from 1.5 µm to 1.7 µm increases the speed by 0.2%.
source: while increasing the length slightly to 1.7 µm increases the speed by 0.2%
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figure 3B.

claim: For cortical axons with constant channel density, the speed at node length 1.7 µm is 24.6% larger than at a node length of 0.43 µm.
source: to a value 24.6% larger than at a node length of 0.43 µm (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is calculated from the modeling results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Along individual axons in the corpus callosum, some variation in node length exists with a mean standard deviation of 0.25 ± 0.06 µm in 18 axons.
source: Although the node length is similar at successive nodes along individual axons (Figure 2B), some variation does exist (with a mean standard deviation of 0.25 ± 0.06 µm in 18 axons)
evidence: This is based on measurements from dye-filled axons shown in Figure 2B.

claim: When the number of channels is held constant and alternate nodes have lengths 0.25 µm shorter and longer than the mean, there is no overall effect on conduction velocity.
source: When the number of channels was held constant at each node, the approximately linear relationship between conduction velocity and node length (Figure 3A,B) resulted in a slightly faster propagation through shorter nodes and a slightly slower propagation through longer nodes, the effects of which cancel out with no overall effect on conduction velocity.
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling considering variable node lengths along an axon.

claim: When the nodal ion channel density is kept constant and alternate nodes have lengths 0.25 µm shorter and longer than the mean, conduction speeds are marginally slower (<2% reduced) compared to when all nodes have exactly the same length.
source: When the nodal ion channel density was kept constant, the concave-downwards dependence of speed on node length in Figure 3A–B resulted in marginally slower conduction speeds (<2% reduced) with variable length nodes, compared to when all the nodes along a particular axon had exactly the same length.
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling considering variable node lengths along an axon.

claim: Internode lengths may vary significantly in the cortex.
source: It has recently been reported that internode lengths may vary significantly in the cortex (Tomassy et al., 2014; Chong et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In rat layer V cortex, internode lengths ranged from 27 µm to 154 µm, with a mean value of 82.7 ± 6.3 µm (30 internodes measured).
source: We measured internode lengths in dye-filled axons in rat layer V cortex by measuring the distance between NaV1.6 positive nodes. Similar to previous studies we found a large variability in the length of 30 internodes, the shortest being 27 µm and the largest 154 µm, with a mean value of 82.7 ± 6.3 µm.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from dye-filled axons.

claim: For cortical axons with constant nodal sodium channel density, the peak of the dependence of conduction speed on node length is displaced to longer node lengths when the internode length is increased.
source: For cortical axons (with a constant nodal sodium channel density), the peak of the dependence of conduction speed on node length is displaced to longer node lengths when the internode length is increased (Figure 3C)
evidence: This is shown by modeling results in Figure 3C.

claim: For cortical axons with constant nodal sodium channel density and internode lengths of 154 µm, the range of node lengths measured could generate changes in conduction speed of up to 42%.
source: and in an axon with internode lengths of 154 µm the range of node lengths measured could generate changes in conduction speed of up to 42%.
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figure 3C.

claim: For cortical axons with constant channel number and short internodes (27 µm), the dependence of conduction speed on node length is greater, resulting in changes in conduction speed of up to 38% over the range of measured node lengths.
source: When the number of channels was held constant at each node, the dependence of conduction speed on node length was greater in axons with short internodes (27 µm), resulting in changes in conduction speed of up to 38% over the range of measured node lengths (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The relationship between conduction speed and internode length rises with internode length at low values of internode length, because more of the axon is myelinated.
source: This relationship rises with internode length at low values of internode length, because more of the axon is myelinated
evidence: This is an explanation of the modeling results shown in Figure 3E,F based on biophysical principles.

claim: The relationship between conduction speed and internode length decreases at large internode lengths as the spread of depolarization between nodes becomes less efficient.
source: but decreases at large internode lengths as the spread of depolarization between nodes becomes less efficient.
evidence: This is an explanation of the modeling results shown in Figure 3E,F based on biophysical principles.

claim: The relationship between conduction speed and internode length shows a sharper peak for shorter node lengths.
source: This relationship shows a sharper peak for shorter node lengths (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is shown by modeling results in Figure 3E,F.

claim: For optic nerve axons with constant nodal conductances, if the number of wraps of myelin is decreased from 7 to 6, the conduction speed is predicted to decrease by 8.6%.
source: With the node length and internode length set at the mean values observed and the nodal conductances constant, if the number of wraps of myelin is decreased by 1 (from the normal 7 to 6 for the optic nerve and from the normal 5 to 4 for the cortex), the conduction speed is predicted to decrease by 8.6% for the optic nerve
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling.

claim: For cortical axons with constant nodal conductances, if the number of wraps of myelin is decreased from 5 to 4, the conduction speed is predicted to decrease by 10.5%.
source: and 10.5% for the cortex
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling.

claim: For optic nerve axons, an 8.6% speed decrease can be achieved by reducing the nodal NaV density by 26%.
source: For comparison, a similar speed decrease is predicted (with no change of wrap number) if the nodal NaV density is reduced by 26% in the optic nerve
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling.

claim: For cortical axons, a 10.5% speed decrease can be achieved by reducing the nodal NaV density by 34%.
source: or 34% in the cortex
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling.

claim: For optic nerve axons, an 8.6% speed decrease can be achieved by increasing the internode length by 36%.
source: or if the internode length is increased by 36% in the optic nerve
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling.

claim: For cortical axons, a 10.5% speed decrease can be achieved by increasing the internode length by 74%.
source: or 74% in the cortex.
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling.

claim: For optic nerve axons, an 8.6% speed decrease can be achieved by decreasing the node length from 1.02 µm to 0.625 µm with no change of myelin wrapping or ion channel density.
source: These same speed decreases can be achieved with no change of myelin wrapping or ion channel density by decreasing the node length from 1.02 µm to 0.625 µm in the optic nerve
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling.

claim: For cortical axons, a 10.5% speed decrease can be achieved by decreasing the node length from 1.5 µm to 0.635 µm with no change of myelin wrapping or ion channel density.
source: or decreasing it from 1.5 µm to 0.635 µm in cortical axons.
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling.

claim: To produce an 8.6% speed change in optic nerve, the change of membrane area needed when altering node length is 1006-fold less than that needed when altering the myelin sheath.
source: Strikingly, to produce these speed changes, the change of membrane area needed (shown in Figure 3G) when altering node length is 1006-fold less in the optic nerve
evidence: This is calculated from the modeling results and shown in Figure 3G.

claim: To produce a 10.5% speed change in cortex, the change of membrane area needed when altering node length is 273-fold less than that needed when altering the myelin sheath.
source: and 273-fold less in the cortex, than that needed when altering the myelin sheath.
evidence: This is calculated from the modeling results and shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Tuning conduction speed by altering node length is far more efficient than altering myelination when considering the amount of lipid and protein synthesis or breakdown needed.
source: Thus, tuning conduction speed by altering node length is far more efficient than altering myelination when considering the amount of lipid and protein synthesis or breakdown needed
evidence: This is inferred from the much smaller membrane area changes needed for node length alterations.

claim: Tuning conduction speed by altering node length would probably be faster than altering myelination.
source: and would probably also be faster.
evidence: This is speculation based on the smaller membrane area changes needed.

claim: Node of Ranvier length may be adjusted to tune axon conduction speed.
source: By combining anatomical measurements with computational modelling we have established a proof of principle for the idea that node of Ranvier length may be adjusted to tune axon conduction speed, and hence alter action potential arrival time.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the combined anatomical and modeling data.

claim: Adjusting node of Ranvier length to tune conduction speed differs from previous ideas on white matter plasticity which have focussed on the effect of changes of myelin thickness and internode length.
source: This differs from previous ideas on white matter plasticity (which have focussed on the effect of changes of myelin thickness and internode length (Fields, 2008; Ullén, 2009))
evidence: This comparison is made with reference to previous literature.

claim: The geometry of the node of Ranvier is a crucial determinant of action potential conduction speed.
source: and demonstrates that the geometry of the node of Ranvier is also a crucial determinant of action potential conduction speed.
evidence: This is concluded from the modeling results showing significant effects of node length on conduction speed.

claim: Even at constant axon diameter, node length displayed a surprising variability, both in the optic nerve and in the grey matter of the cortex.
source: Even at constant axon diameter, we found that node length displayed a surprising variability, both in the optic nerve and in the grey matter of the cortex (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on the anatomical measurements presented in Figure 1.

claim: Node length variation was largely between different axons, while the nodes on any given axon tended to have similar lengths.
source: Remarkably, this node length variation was largely between different axons, while the nodes on any given axon tended to have similar lengths (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on the anatomical measurements presented in Figure 2.

claim: The range of node lengths observed is sufficient to produce large variations in action potential conduction speed comparable to those produced by adding or removing a wrap of myelin.
source: The range of node lengths observed is sufficient to produce large variations in action potential conduction speed (Figure 3), comparable to those produced by adding or removing a wrap of myelin.
evidence: This is based on the modeling results presented in Figure 3.

claim: Axons may be able to adjust their node lengths in order to tune their conduction speed, and thus the arrival time of the information that they transmit.
source: These data suggest that axons may be able to adjust their node lengths in order to tune their conduction speed, and thus the arrival time of the information that they transmit.
evidence: This is speculation based on the combined anatomical and modeling data.

claim: There is evidence of oligodendrogenesis and myelination in the adult CNS.
source: There is now evidence of oligodendrogenesis and myelination in the adult CNS (Dimou et al., 2008; Young et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Oligodendrogenesis and myelination in the adult CNS presumably results in the formation of new nodes of Ranvier.
source: which presumably results in the formation of new nodes of Ranvier.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the process of myelination.

claim: NaV1.6 is a marker of mature nodes.
source: To avoid these, we studied only nodes that expressed the mature node marker NaV1.6 (Boiko et al., 2001; Kaplan et al., 2001)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The variability in node length observed across a large fraction of the nodes measured makes it improbable that this variation is solely due to nodes being at different developmental stages.
source: and the fact that the variability in node length was observed across a large fraction of the nodes measured makes it improbable that this variation is solely due to nodes being at different developmental stages.
evidence: This is inferred from the widespread nature of the variability observed.

claim: Node length may mainly be adjusted by the insertion or removal of membrane containing sodium channels.
source: suggesting that node length may mainly be adjusted by the insertion or removal of membrane containing sodium channels
evidence: This is inferred from the proportionality between node length and sodium channel labeling.

claim: It is conceivably possible to vary node length in a manner independent of sodium channel trafficking by endo- or exocytosis of vesicles lacking sodium channels in their membrane.
source: (although conceivably it is possible to vary node length in a manner independent of sodium channel trafficking by endo- or exocytosis of vesicles lacking sodium channels in their membrane).
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative mechanism.

claim: Node length regulation may involve modifying the paranodal cell adhesion between the myelin and the axon, mediated by the molecules Caspr, neurofascin 155 and contactin.
source: Node length regulation may involve modifying the paranodal cell adhesion between the myelin and the axon, mediated by the molecules Caspr, neurofascin 155 and contactin
evidence: This is speculation based on known molecular components of the node.

claim: Node length regulation may involve altering ankyrin G mediated scaffolding within the axon that locates voltage-gated Na+ channels at the node.
source: as well as altering ankyrin G mediated scaffolding within the axon that locates voltage-gated Na+ channels at the node (Arancibia-Carcamo and Attwell, 2014).
evidence: This is speculation based on known molecular components of the node, with reference to a review.

claim: Nodal amyloid precursor protein has been proposed as a regulator of node length.
source: Interestingly, nodal amyloid precursor protein has been proposed as a regulator of node length (Xu et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Changes in the processing of amyloid precursor protein could alter node length in Alzheimer's disease.
source: prompting the speculation that changes in the processing of this molecule could alter node length in Alzheimer's disease.
evidence: This is speculation based on the proposed role of amyloid precursor protein in node length regulation.

claim: The range of node lengths seen in the optic nerve (0.5–2.2 µm) can alter the conduction speed by up to 20% for a constant nodal channel density.
source: The range of node lengths seen in the optic nerve (0.5–2.2 µm) can alter the conduction speed by up to 20% (for a constant nodal channel density in Figure 3A)
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The range of node lengths seen in the cortex (0.43–3.7 µm) can produce a change of up to 25% in axons with 82 µm long internodes for a constant density of nodal channels.
source: while the range seen in the cortex (0.43–3.7 µm) can produce a larger change of up to 25% (for a constant density of nodal channels in Figure 3B) in axons with 82 µm long internodes
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The range of node lengths seen in the cortex can produce a change of up to 38% for axons with 27 µm long internodes when the number of channels is held constant at each node.
source: or 38% for axons with 27 µm long internodes (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The effect of altering node length is larger in cortical axons than in the optic nerve, partly because the 1.5-fold longer nodes contribute a larger fraction of the total axon capacitance in the cortex where the internodes are also 1.7-fold shorter.
source: The effect of altering node length is larger in cortical axons than in the optic nerve, partly because the 1.5-fold longer nodes contribute a larger fraction of the total axon capacitance in the cortex where the internodes are also 1.7-fold shorter.
evidence: This is an explanation based on the geometrical parameters used in the model.

claim: Modulation of node length could be a viable strategy for adjusting the propagation time of action potentials to meet information processing needs.
source: Our data and simulations suggest that modulation of node length could be a viable strategy for adjusting the propagation time of action potentials to meet information processing needs.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined anatomical and modeling data.

claim: For an intercortical callosal axon of length 1 cm in rat with the properties assumed in the simulations, a 20% decrease of axon conduction speed would increase the time needed to propagate information between the cortices from 3.8 to 4.8 ms.
source: For an intercortical callosal axon of length 1 cm (in rat) or 6 cm (in human), with the properties that we assume for our simulations, a 20% decrease of axon conduction speed (from the value occurring for the mean observed node length) would increase the time needed to propagate information between the cortices from 3.8 to 4.8 ms in rat
evidence: This is calculated from the modeling results.

claim: For an intercortical callosal axon of length 6 cm in human with the properties assumed in the simulations, a 20% decrease of axon conduction speed would increase the time needed to propagate information between the cortices from 23 to 29 ms.
source: and from 23 to 29 ms in humans.
evidence: This is calculated from the modeling results.

claim: Chronic stress and major depression shorten the node.
source: Such modulation has been suggested to occur during chronic stress and major depression (Miyata et al., 2016) which shorten the node
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: High frequency action potential activity lengthens the node.
source: as well as high frequency action potential activity (Huff et al., 2011; Trigo and Smith, 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Acoustic over-exposure lengthens the node.
source: acoustic over-exposure (Tagoe et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Pathological release of glutamate lengthens the node.
source: pathological release of glutamate (Fu et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Hypoxic conditions lengthen the node.
source: and hypoxic conditions (Reimer et al., 2011), all of which lengthen the node.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Altering node length offers the advantage that very small changes of membrane area, which could easily be produced rapidly by exocytosis or endocytosis at the node, produce large changes of conduction speed.
source: Altering node length offers the advantage that very small changes of membrane area, which could easily be produced rapidly by exocytosis or endocytosis at the node, produce large changes of conduction speed.
evidence: This is inferred from the modeling results showing large speed changes with small membrane area changes.

claim: To produce the same speed changes by altering the number of myelin wraps requires the energetically expensive synthesis or disassembly of a membrane area that is 273–1006 fold larger than for node length changes.
source: In comparison, to produce the same speed changes by altering the number of myelin wraps requires the energetically expensive (Harris and Attwell, 2012), and probably more time consuming, synthesis or disassembly of a membrane area that is 273–1006 fold larger.
evidence: This is calculated from the modeling results, with reference to previous literature on energy costs.

claim: Both node length alteration and myelin wrap alteration mechanisms might be used on different time scales.
source: In practice, both mechanisms might be used on different time scales.
evidence: This is speculation about how these mechanisms might be employed.

claim: Mature nodes of Ranvier were identified from their NaV1.6 staining flanked by Caspr-labelled paranodes.
source: Mature nodes of Ranvier were identified from their NaV1.6 staining (a marker of mature nodes: Boiko et al., 2001; Kaplan et al., 2001) flanked by Caspr-labelled paranodes (Figure 1A)
evidence: This describes the experimental method used, with citations supporting NaV1.6 as a mature node marker.

claim: Node length was measured from the Caspr intensity profile across the node.
source: and node length was measured from the Caspr intensity profile across the node (Figure 1B, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used.

claim: The model implemented was model C of Richardson et al. (2000) at 37°C.
source: To simulate action potential propagation along myelinated axons, we implemented, in MATLAB, model C of Richardson et al. (2000) (at 37°C, with the unphysiologically low membrane capacitance of Richardson et al. (2000) corrected to a normal value).
evidence: This describes the computational model used, with citation to the original model.

claim: The differential equations of the model were derived and solved as in Halter and Clark (1991).
source: The differential equations of the model were derived and solved as in Halter and Clark (1991).
evidence: This describes the computational method used, with citation to the original method.

claim: The model includes fast and persistent Na+, and slow K+, voltage-gated channels at the node.
source: This model includes fast and persistent Na+, and slow K+, voltage-gated channels at the node
evidence: This describes a feature of the computational model.

claim: The model omits voltage-gated K+ channels at the juxtaparanode because they are little activated.
source: but omits voltage-gated K+ channels at the juxtaparanode (which are little activated because the 100 mV voltage change of the action potential is distributed across the 11–15 membranes of the 5–7 myelin wraps and the axon, implying only a 7–9 mV voltage change across the axonal membrane).
evidence: This describes a simplification in the computational model with biophysical justification.

claim: If node shortening by X µm requires an X µm elongation of the myelin sheath, the sheath membrane area increase is larger than the area decrease at the node by a factor of 2x(number of myelin wraps)x(mean radius of wraps)/(node radius), which is roughly 18.4 for the optic nerve and 13 for the cortex.
source: One can show mathematically that the sheath membrane area increase is larger than the area decrease at the node by a factor of 2x(number of myelin wraps)x(mean radius of wraps)/(node radius), which is roughly 18.4 for the optic nerve and 13 for the cortex.
evidence: This is a mathematical calculation based on the geometrical parameters of the model.

claim: Accounting for membrane area changes when the internode is lengthened as the node is shortened would reduce the ratio of membrane area changes needed (when adding a layer of myelin versus changing node length) from 1006-fold to 55-fold for the optic nerve and from 273-fold to 21-fold for the cortex.
source: Accounting for these area changes (and noting that, in this situation, there is no change of total axon length) would reduce the ratio of the membrane area changes needed to produce a given speed change (when adding a layer of myelin to the sheath versus changing the node length) from 1006-fold to 55-fold for the optic nerve and from 273-fold to 21-fold for the cortex
evidence: This is calculated from the modeling results considering additional membrane changes.

claim: Even when accounting for internode lengthening, the ratios of membrane area changes (55-fold and 21-fold) remain impressively large, and the energetic argument favouring speed tuning by alteration of node length still holds.
source: but these ratios remain impressively large, and so the energetic argument favouring speed tuning by alteration of the node length still holds.
evidence: This is concluded from the calculated ratios even under the more conservative assumptions.
